title: Cicero Mourns His Daughter Tullia
text:
Marcus Tullius Cicero, orator and statesman, loved his daughter Tullia more than anyone. His letters call her his darling and his delight. Her marriages were unlucky. Her third husband, Dolabella, was unfaithful and spendthrift, and they divorced. In January 45 BC she gave birth to a son, and a month later, in February, she died at Cicero's villa at Tusculum.

Cicero was shattered. He retreated alone to his villa at Astura on the coast, where he spent his days walking in the woods and reading every book of consolation he could find. He wrote a consolation addressed to himself, the first of its kind, and made plans to build a shrine in her memory. In his letters to his friend Atticus he admitted that nothing helped: reading and writing calmed him only for a time.

His friend Servius Sulpicius sent him a famous letter of comfort from Greece. Sailing from Aegina towards Megara, he wrote, he had looked around at Aegina, Megara, Piraeus and Corinth, once flourishing cities now lying in ruins, and asked himself how short-lived humans could protest when one of them died. He reminded Cicero that Tullia had lived as long as life had anything to give her.

Cicero replied gratefully but honestly. Before, he wrote, when public life went badly, he found refuge at home with his daughter. Now he had no refuge at all.
lesson: Grief for a child does not yield to arguments, even a philosopher's. A friend's words help most when they keep us company rather than ask us to stop grieving.
people: Marcus Tullius Cicero, Tullia, Servius Sulpicius Rufus, Atticus
source: Cicero, Letters to Atticus, book 12; Letters to Friends 4.5 (Sulpicius) and 4.6 (Cicero's reply)
